questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about a price ceiling is false?

options.A: Effective price ceiling creates an excess demand
options.B: Effective price ceiling decreases producer surplus
options.C: To have any effect, the price ceiling must be set at a lower level than the original equilibrium price.
options.D: Effective price ceiling creates an excess supply

questions.explanation: An effective (binding) price ceiling is set below the market equilibrium price, causing quantity demanded to exceed quantity supplied, thereby creating an excess demand (shortage), not an excess supply.

questions.question_text: When a market is in equilibrium, the buyers are those with the _______ willingness to pay and the sellers are those with the ___________ costs.
questions.explanation: Market equilibrium efficiently allocates goods to the consumers who value them the most (highest willingness to pay) and to the producers who can produce them at the lowest cost.

questions.question_text: On 1st of March 2026, in an attempt to commit to getting fit, I signed a year-long, binding contract at a local gym, and paid Rs 6000 in yearly membership fees. I also spent Rs 2000 on extremely stylish gym clothes. This morning on May 23rd 2026, I was trying to decide whether or not to actually go to the gym. Which of the following was relevant to this decision?

options.A: The Rs 6000 that I paid towards gym membership.
options.B: The Rs 2000 I spent on gym clothes.
options.C: The fact that I also had to write a BBA DBE Final exam today.
options.D: All of the above were relevant.

questions.explanation: The gym membership fee (Rs. 6,000) and the cost of gym clothes (Rs. 2,000) are sunk costs since they have already been paid and cannot be recovered. Only the opportunity cost of time (such as writing the BBA DBE Final exam today) is relevant to the decision.

questions.question_text:
A buyer has purchased three units of good X. The marginal benefit of the fourth unit of X exceeds the marginal cost of the fourth unit of good X. Which of the following reasons explains why the buyer should purchase the fourth unit?
I. The marginal net benefit of the fourth unit is positive.
II. Buying the fourth unit will increase total benefits by more than total costs.
III. Buying the fourth unit will increase total benefits and decrease total costs.
questions.explanation: Since the marginal benefit of the 4th unit exceeds its marginal cost ($MB > MC$), the marginal net benefit ($MB - MC$) is positive (Statement I), and total benefits will increase by more than total costs (Statement II). Buying another unit increases total costs, making Statement III false.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the diagram below, which illustrates a consumer's demand curve for a good

PARSEIMAGE

If the price of this good is Rs. 30, what quantity will be demanded?
questions.explanation: According to the demand curve, when the price is Rs. 30, the corresponding quantity on the horizontal axis is 5 units.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the diagram in Question 5.

If the price of this good is Rs. 20, what will consumer surplus equal?
questions.explanation:
Consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price level of Rs. 20. This forms a triangle with height = $40 - 20 = 20$ and base = 10. 
$$\text{Consumer Surplus} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100$$

questions.question_text:
Refer to the diagram in Question 5.

If the price of this good fall from Rs. 30 to Rs. 20, but the consumer is prohibited from buying more than 5 units of the good, by how much will consumer surplus increase?
questions.explanation: When the price falls from Rs. 30 to Rs. 20, the consumer continues to buy 5 units due to the quantity restriction. The consumer surplus on each of these 5 units increases by the price drop of Rs. 10 ($30 - 20$). Thus, consumer surplus increases by $5 \text{ units} \times \text{Rs. } 10 = \text{Rs. } 50$.

questions.question_text:
An economic consultant estimates the demand function for a product as:
$$Q_x^d = 8000 - 2 P_x + 5 P_y + 0.5 I$$

Where,
$Q_x$ is quantity demanded,
$P_x$ is price of good X,
$P_y$ is price of related good Y, and
$I$ is income.

Which of the following is correct?

options.A: Goods X and Y are complements, and X is an inferior good.
options.B: Goods X and Y are substitutes, and X is a normal good.
options.C: Goods X and Y are complements, and X is a normal good.
options.D: Goods X and Y are substitutes, and X is an inferior good.

questions.explanation: Since the coefficient of $P_y$ is positive ($+5$), an increase in the price of Y increases demand for X, meaning they are substitutes. Since the coefficient of $I$ is positive ($+0.5$), an increase in income increases demand for X, indicating X is a normal good.

questions.question_text: If cookies are a normal good and incomes increase, we would expect:

options.A: A decrease in equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
options.B: An increase in equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
options.C: An increase in equilibrium price and a decrease in equilibrium quantity.
options.D: A decrease in equilibrium price and an increase in equilibrium quantity.

questions.explanation: For a normal good, an increase in income shifts the demand curve to the right, leading to a higher equilibrium price and a higher equilibrium quantity.

questions.question_text: Sarah is selling her used truck. The minimum price at which she is willing to sell her truck is Rs. 5,000. She advertises the truck on olx.com for Rs. 8,000, and eventually sells the truck for Rs 6,000. Her producer surplus is equal to _____.
questions.explanation: Producer surplus is the actual price received minus the minimum price the seller is willing to accept. Therefore, $\text{Producer Surplus} = 6,000 - 5,000 = \text{Rs. 1,000}$.

questions.question_text:
The figure below shows three different demand and supply graphs. Which graph best represents the market for vacation on planet Mars today?

PARSEIMAGE
questions.explanation: Since space travel is currently too expensive for ordinary consumers, the cost of supply (S) lies entirely above the willingness to pay (D), meaning there is no intersection and no market currently exists. Graph A represents this situation.

questions.question_text: Suppose you are told that the own-price elasticity of supply equal 0.5. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of this number?

options.A: A 1% increase in price will result in a 0.5% increase in quantity supplied.
options.B: A 1% increase in price will result in a 50% increase in quantity supplied.
options.C: A 1% increase in price will result in a 2% increase in quantity supplied.
options.D: A 1% increase in price will result in a 5% increase in quantity supplied.

questions.explanation: Price elasticity of supply measures the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price. Thus, a value of 0.5 means a 1% increase in price leads to a $0.5 \times 1\% = 0.5\%$ increase in quantity supplied.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand curves illustrated below.

PARSEIMAGE

A price ceiling of P3 causes:

options.A: A deadweight loss triangle whose corners are ACD.
options.B: A deadweight loss triangle whose corners are CDE.
options.C: A deadweight loss triangle whose corners are BEC.
options.D: A deadweight loss triangle whose corners are ABC.

questions.explanation: A binding price ceiling at $P_3$ reduces the quantity traded to $Q_1$. The lost economic surplus is represented by the deadweight loss triangle ACD, bounded by the demand curve, supply curve, and quantity limit line at $Q_1$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand curves in Question 13.

A price floor of P1 causes:

options.A: Excess supply equal to the distance AB.
options.B: Excess supply equal to the distance DE.
options.C: Excess demand equal to the distance AB.
options.D: Excess demand equal to the distance DE.

questions.explanation: A price floor at $P_1$ is above the equilibrium price $P_2$. At $P_1$, quantity demanded is at point A ($Q_1$) and quantity supplied is at point B ($Q_3$). This results in an excess supply (surplus) represented by the horizontal distance AB.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand curves illustrated below.

PARSEIMAGE

Consider the introduction of a Rs. 10 per unit tax in this market.

Which areas represent the loss to Consumer AND Producer Surplus as a result of this tax?
questions.explanation: The tax reduces both consumer surplus (by area $k + f$) and producer surplus (by area $j + g$). Thus, the combined loss to both consumer and producer surplus is represented by the area $k + f + j + g$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand curves in Question 15.

Which areas represent the gain in government revenue as a result of this tax?
questions.explanation: Government tax revenue is calculated as the tax per unit (represented by the height of the wedge) multiplied by the quantity traded after tax ($Q_2$). This is represented by the rectangle $k + j$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand equations illustrated below
A market is described by:
$$Q^s = 2P, \quad Q^d = 300 - P$$
The government imposes a per-unit tax of Rs. 30 on producers.

If P is the per-unit price paid by the consumers. What is the new supply curve after the tax?
questions.explanation: With a tax of Rs. 30 imposed on producers, the price received by producers ($P_s$) is the price paid by consumers ($P$) minus the tax ($P - 30$). Substituting $P_s = P - 30$ into the original supply equation gives $Q^s = 2(P - 30)$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand equations in Question 17.

What is the new equilibrium price paid by consumers and quantity traded?
questions.explanation:
To find the new equilibrium, equate the new supply and demand equations: 
$$2(P - 30) = 300 - P \implies 2P - 60 = 300 - P \implies 3P = 360 \implies P_c = 120$$
Substituting $P_c = 120$ into the demand equation yields $Q = 300 - 120 = 180$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand equations in Question 17.

What is the price received by producers after tax?
questions.explanation: The price received by producers ($P_s$) after tax is the price paid by consumers ($P_c = 120$) minus the per-unit tax (Rs. 30). Thus, $P_s = 120 - 30 = \text{Rs. } 90$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand equations in Question 17.

What is the government's tax revenue?
questions.explanation: Government tax revenue is the per-unit tax (Rs. 30) multiplied by the equilibrium quantity traded after tax ($Q = 180$). Thus, $\text{Revenue} = 30 \times 180 = \text{Rs. } 5,400$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the supply and demand equations in Question 17.

What is the deadweight loss (DWL) due to the tax?
questions.explanation:
The pre-tax equilibrium is $2P = 300 - P \implies P^* = 100$, $Q^* = 200$. The tax reduces quantity to 180. 
$$\text{DWL} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Tax} \times (Q^* - Q_{\text{tax}}) = \frac{1}{2} \times 30 	imes (200 - 180) = \text{Rs. 300}$$

questions.question_text:
Consider the supply and demand diagram below. Assume that:
(i) there are no externalities; and
(ii) in the absence of government regulation, the market supply curve is the one labelled $S_1$.

PARSEIMAGE

If a $5 per unit tax is introduced in this market, which area represents the deadweight loss?
questions.explanation: The introduction of the tax shifts the supply curve from $S_1$ to $S_2$. The deadweight loss is represented by the triangle bounded by the demand curve, the original supply curve $S_1$, and the post-tax quantity line of 60, which consists of areas $b$ and $c$.

questions.question_text:
The following table shows the relationship between labour and output for a firm.

| Quantity of Labour | Total Output |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 12 |
| 2 | 25 |
| 3 | 36 |
| 4 | 40 |
| 5 | 43 |

Recall marginal product of labour is the additional output obtained by increasing the labour by one unit. The marginal product of the fourth unit of labour hired is:
questions.explanation:
The marginal product of the 4th worker is the change in total output when going from 3 to 4 workers:
$$\text{MP} = \text{Total Output}_4 - \text{Total Output}_3 = 40 - 36 = 4 \text{ units}$$

questions.question_text:
Refer to the table in Question 23.

If each unit of labour must be paid a wage of Rs.10, then what do (total) variable costs equal, at an output level of 25 units?
questions.explanation: To produce 25 units of output, the firm requires 2 units of labor (as shown in the table). Since each unit of labor is paid Rs. 10, the total variable cost is $2 \times 10 = \text{Rs. } 20$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the table in Question 23.

If three workers are employed, then the average product of labour is:
questions.explanation:
Average product of labor is total output divided by the quantity of labor:
$$\text{AP} = \frac{\text{Total Output}}{\text{Labour}} = \frac{36}{3} = 12$$

questions.question_text: If the marginal cost of producing output is constant and equal to Rs. 5 per unit, and fixed costs are equal to Rs. 600, then average total cost given an output level of 100 is:
questions.explanation: Since marginal cost is constant at Rs. 5, the total variable cost for 100 units is $100 \times 5 = 500$. Total cost is $FC + VC = 600 + 500 = 1100$. Average total cost is $\frac{1100}{100} = \text{Rs. } 11$.

questions.question_text:
The below diagram, illustrates a competitive firm's cost curves.

PARSEIMAGE

What do this firm's fixed costs equal?

options.D: There is insufficient information to calculate the firm’s fixed costs.

questions.explanation: At $Q = 5$, $\text{ATC} = 10$ and $\text{AVC} = 4$. Since $\text{ATC} = \text{AVC} + \text{AFC}$, we have $\text{AFC} = 10 - 4 = 6$. Thus, the fixed cost is $\text{FC} = \text{AFC} \times Q = 6 \times 5 = 30$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the cost curves in Question 27.

The average fixed cost at output level 15 is:
questions.explanation: At $Q = 15$, $\text{ATC} = 7$ and $\text{AVC} = 5$. The average fixed cost is the difference between average total cost and average variable cost: $\text{AFC} = 7 - 5 = \text{Rs. } 2$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the cost curves in Question 27.

If the market price is Rs. 5 per unit, then the firm’s short run profits are ___________.
questions.explanation: At a market price of Rs. 5, the price is above the minimum average variable cost (which is Rs. 4). Therefore, the firm will produce a positive quantity in the short run where $P = MC > AVC$, yielding positive short-run operating profit ($TR - TVC > 0$).

questions.question_text:
Refer to the cost curves in Question 27.

If the market price is Rs. 10 per unit, then the firm’s short-run profit is equal to:
questions.explanation: At a price of Rs. 10, the profit-maximizing quantity where $P = MC$ is $Q = 15$. At this output, the average variable cost (AVC) is Rs. 5. Short-run profit (operating profit) is $(P - AVC) \times Q = (10 - 5) \times 15 = \text{Rs. } 75$.

questions.question_text:
Suppose that a firm operating in a perfectly competitive market is currently producing 10 units of output. You also have the following additional information:
$$P = \text{Rs. } 6; \quad MC = \text{Rs. } 6; \quad AVC = \text{Rs. } 3; \quad ATC = \text{Rs. } 8.$$

Given this:

options.A: This firm should increase its output in order to maximize profits.
options.B: This firm should continue to produce 10 units in the short run
options.C: This firm should shut down in the short run
options.D: This firm should increase its price in order to maximize profits.

questions.explanation: Since $P = MC = 6$, the firm is maximizing its profit (minimizing its loss) at the current output of 10 units. Because the price ($P = 6$) is greater than average variable cost ($AVC = 3$), the firm should continue to produce in the short run rather than shut down, even though it is making an economic loss ($P < ATC$).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about a firm operating in a perfectly competitive market is FALSE?

options.A: A competitive firm maximizes profit by producing the level of output at which price equal marginal cost.
options.B: For a competitive firm, economic profits equal zero in the long run.
options.C: A competitive firm maximizes profit by producing the level of output at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
options.D: For a competitive firm, marginal revenue is less than price.

questions.explanation: In a perfectly competitive market, firms are price takers, meaning they can sell any quantity at the market price. Thus, marginal revenue is always equal to price ($MR = P$), making statement D false.

questions.question_text: A monopolist faces a downward sloping demand curve. At the monopolist’s current output choice, marginal cost equals price. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: We do not have enough information to know whether or not the monopolist is maximizing profits.
options.B: The monopolist is currently maximizing profits.
options.C: The monopolist should produce less output to maximize profits.
options.D: The monopolist should produce more output to maximize profits.

questions.explanation: For a monopolist facing a downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue is less than price ($MR < P$). If the monopolist is producing where $MC = P$, then $MC > MR$. To maximize profits, the firm must decrease output until $MR = MC$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the diagram below, which illustrates the demand, marginal revenue, and marginal cost curves for a profit-maximizing single-price monopolist.

PARSEIMAGE

Which area represents the deadweight loss due to the monopoly?
questions.explanation: The deadweight loss of a monopoly is the lost gains from trade because the monopolist restricts output below the socially efficient level (where $P = MC$). This is represented by the triangle bounded by the demand curve, marginal cost curve, and the monopoly quantity line, which consists of areas $g$ and $h$.

questions.question_text:
Refer to the diagram in Question 34.

Which area represents the monopolist's producer surplus?
questions.explanation: Producer surplus is the area below the price charged by the monopolist and above the marginal cost curve, up to the quantity produced. In the diagram, this is represented by the sum of areas $a + b + f + c + j$.

questions.question_text: If demand for cigarettes is inelastic and supply is relatively elastic, who will bear a larger burden of a per-unit tax?

options.A: The tax burden is split equally
options.B: Producers, since they face cost increases
options.D: Consumers, because they are less responsive to price

questions.explanation: The burden of a tax falls more heavily on the side of the market that is less elastic (more inelastic). Since demand for cigarettes is inelastic and supply is elastic, consumers are less responsive to price changes and will bear the larger share of the tax burden.

questions.question_text: If the price of tea rises by 10% and the quantity demanded for coffee rises by 5%, the cross elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation:
Cross-price elasticity of demand is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded of coffee divided by the percentage change in the price of tea: 
$$\text{Cross Elasticity} = \frac{+5\%}{+10\%} = 0.5$$

questions.question_text: When both demand and supply increase simultaneously, equilibrium price:

options.D: May rise, fall, or remain constant

questions.explanation: An increase in demand shifts the demand curve right, which tends to raise the price. An increase in supply shifts the supply curve right, which tends to lower the price. Because these two forces work in opposite directions on price, the net effect on equilibrium price is ambiguous.

questions.question_text: The vertical distance between AC and AVC curves equals:
questions.explanation: Since Average Total Cost ($ATC$, or $AC$) is the sum of Average Fixed Cost ($AFC$) and Average Variable Cost ($AVC$), the vertical distance between them ($ATC - AVC$) is exactly equal to the Average Fixed Cost ($AFC$).

questions.question_text: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 - 2Q. Find MR.
questions.explanation: For a linear inverse demand curve of the form $P = A - BQ$, the marginal revenue curve has the same intercept and twice the slope: $MR = A - 2BQ$. Thus, for $P = 100 - 2Q$, the marginal revenue is $MR = 100 - 4Q$.
